dialogs.title: დიალოგი — Weekend plans
dialogs.intro: Levan calls Ani to ask her out. The dialogue is full of future forms — don't try to take them apart yet; just get to know what they mean.

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: Ani, are you free on Saturday?

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: I have class in the morning, but I'm free after that.
lines.literal: morning-by — lesson — I-have, then — free — I-am.

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: Great. Shall we go up Mtatsminda? You can see the whole city from there.
lines.literal: Mtatsminda-on — let's-go-up? there-from — whole — city — is-visible.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: I'd love to! What time shall we meet?

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: She can't, she works on Saturday. But she's free on Sunday.
lines.literal: can't, Saturday-on — she-works. Sunday-on — though — free-is.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Then shall the three of us meet on Sunday?

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: Perfect! On Sunday lunch is on me.

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: That's not how it works in Georgia, Ani!

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Fine, but next time I'm paying!

notes: **"Let's…" is formed with the -ოთ / -ეთ ending, and you've been seeing it since unit 3.** წავიდე**თ** (let's go), ავიდე**თ** (let's go up), შევხვდე**თ** (let's meet), ვნახო**თ** (let's see), გადავიხადო**თ** (let's pay). They all mean "let's…" and need no extra word.
**Another way to invite that's easier for beginners: გინდა…?** *გინდა კინოში წავიდეთ?* (want to see a movie?), *გინდა ყავა დავლიოთ?* (want to grab a coffee?). This pattern is safe for anything.

**ვერა is not არა.** ⚠️ To say no because you **can't** — you have other plans, you're working — use **ვერ**/**ვერა**, not არ/არა. *ვერ მოვალ* = I can't come. *არ მოვალ* = I won't come, and that sounds rude. The difference matters most in social sentences like these.
**სიამოვნებით = "with pleasure".** The standard answer for accepting any invitation. Notice the -ით ending you already know: სიამოვნება (pleasure) → სიამოვნებ**ით**.

**The future at A1: recognize it, don't build it yet.** მოვა (he/she will come), მოვალ (I'll come), ვნახავ (I'll see), ვიყიდი (I'll buy), ვიქნები (I'll be). It's formed with prefixes that differ from verb to verb and can't be guessed — that's A2 work. For now, the ten verbs at the back of this book are enough.

**About who pays.** ⚠️ This isn't just small talk. In Georgia, the person who **invites** almost always pays, and refusing too hard is actually seen as rude. The right way out isn't to insist on paying now, but to say *შემდეგში მე ვიხდი* (next time I'm paying) — and keep your word.

**მთაწმინდა (Mtatsminda) is the hill above Tbilisi**, reached by funicular (ფუნიკულიორი). You can see the whole city from up there, and it's the first meeting spot Tbilisi locals most often suggest to guests.

blocks.title: Canceling without hurting the friendship
items: **ბოდიში, ვერ მოვალ.** — Sorry, I can't come. (the core sentence; no need for more)
**შეიძლება სხვა დროს?** — Could we do it another time?
**ხვალ დაგირეკავ.** (khval dagirek'av) — I'll call you tomorrow.
⚠️ Canceling by text without offering another time comes across as cold. Always add the third or fourth sentence above.

blocks.text: One thing worth knowing from the start: Georgian invitations often sound sudden and are often **not** just politeness. *ხვალ ჩვენთან მოდი* (come to our place tomorrow) from someone you met a week ago is a real invitation, and turning it down again and again will be taken as rejecting the person, not the plan. If you really can't, offer another time — that's what separates "I can't today" from "I don't want to".

items: I can't come, I have class → ____ მოვალ
I don't eat pork → ღორის ხორცს ____ ვჭამ
I can't speak Georgian well → ____ ვლაპარაკობ კარგად
